known_gaps: San Diego was substituted for San Jose, the originally assigned 'own checklist' city, because the entire sanjoseca.gov domain returned HTTP 403 (Akamai edge block) to every fetch attempt and Wayback lookups were rate-limited. San Diego has a far richer directly fetchable trail, but it is a different market (SDG&E rather than PG&E territory) and the substitution should be carried into any cross-jurisdiction comparison.

The observed permit median contradicts the declared design and nothing here resolves it. San Diego advertises a self-issued, no-plan-review permit, yet SolarTRACE's 2023 median AHJ permit time for the city is 14 business days -- the slowest of California's high-volume AHJs. Nothing in IB 301, the User Guide or the program page explains the gap. Candidate explanations that the corpus cannot separate: SolarTRACE pools all PV permit types at AHJ level (so plan-review-tier and building-permit projects are mixed in), the Scout pre-validation and 'Updates Required' loop may consume calendar time before a reviewable submittal exists, or 2023 was a NEM 2.0 deadline surge year. Which of these dominates is the single biggest unsettled question in this model.

San Diego's own documents disagree about how many inspections are required. The Inspection Guidelines list rough electrical, array bonding/grounding and final for roof-mounted systems, and IB 301 enumerates up to six possible inspections, while Gov. Code 65850.5(h) requires only one consolidated inspection for an expedited-eligible small system and SolarTRACE records 'Number of Inspections Required' = 1 with no rough-in for the AHJ. A13's existence on the self-issued path is therefore genuinely uncertain.

SDG&E's residential PTO process is undocumented end to end. No SDG&E page states a residential PTO turnaround, no residential interconnection fee is published, and the internal review steps between application and energization approval are invisible. A19-A22 are the thinnest-evidenced activities in this model; the $800 Interconnection Request Fee on SDG&E's Rule 21 page belongs to exporting Rule 21 generator projects and was deliberately not assigned to A19.

The published fee and the observed fee differ. IB 301 sets the no-plan-review inspection fee at $275.80; SolarTRACE records San Diego's median residential 1-10 kW permit cost as $268.80. The gap is small but means fee error is scorable against two defensible targets.

CPUC Decision D.20-09-035 requires each IOU to report interconnection timeline metrics quarterly, but the CPUC's own page states it 'did not mandate reporting for net energy metering (NEM) systems smaller than 30 kVA' -- exactly the residential population modelled here. The richest potential observed dataset on SDG&E's interconnection speed is therefore structurally absent.

Several one-hop applicant documents were not fetched within budget: the Residential Solar PV Project Plan Template, the PDF document requirements, and the 'How to Schedule Inspection for PV Systems' sheet. The last of these is the one place a San Diego inspection-scheduling SLA might exist; A12's timing is null because of it.

San Diego runs no SolarAPP+ integration at all, so this model has no automated-platform counterpart to Oakland's A03/A05. That absence is the intended disentanglement contrast between the two city models and should not be scored as a missing activity.
notes: Why this is the gold for San Diego: the city publishes its designed tier almost in full. IB 301 (fee schedule, service tiers, review triggers, inspection list), the electronic-submittal User Guide (the 'Updates Required' and 'Recheck Required' rework states, the Project Issues Report, the Scout gate) and the Inspection Guidelines (per-section inspector checklist, placard duties, the 2:00 p.m. outage choreography) together expose procedure that most jurisdictions keep internal. The consequence is a deliberate and informative asymmetry against the Oakland model: San Diego has exactly one staff_only activity (A23, the CEC filings), because almost everything else a solver would expect to be hidden is in a published bulletin. Three structural points. (1) The self-issued design means there is no approval decision on the main path -- A05 flows straight to A10 and the permit issues on payment -- so the plan-review activities (A07-A09) are genuinely optional branches, not the spine. (2) The permit track and the interconnection track are legally distinct under Gov. Code 65850.52(g), and A18 is the seam; uniquely among these three models the City, not the contractor, is described as notifying the utility, but IB 301 says so in a passive construction that names no actor and no latency. (3) The declared design and the observed record openly conflict on both permit speed (self-issued vs a 14-business-day 2023 median) and inspection count (one consolidated inspection in statute and SolarTRACE vs a multi-stage sequence in the city's own guidelines); both conflicts are preserved rather than reconciled, and are flagged in known_gaps as scoring targets. gold_tier is 'designed+observed' because the graph is designed-tier while every timing figure is records-derived; per-tier scoring should treat the process model as designed-only.
